The only way l(K - D) = g under this constraint is if g = 0 . ◻ Existence of Low Degree Morphisms to \mathbb{P}^1 and Hyperelliptic Curves Proposition 1.1 (Existence of Low Degree Morphisms to \mathbb{P}^1 ). Let X be a complete nonsingular curve of genus g over a field k . Then there exists a finite morphism f: X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k of degree \le g + 1 . Proof. Let P \in X be a k -rational point of the curve (if no k -rational point exists, one can work with a closed point P and clear the residue field degree, but let us assume for a standard divisor argument we use a closed point P of degree d_P ). To construct a morphism to \mathbb{P}^1_k of degree n \cdot \deg P , it suffices to find a divisor D = nP such that l(nD) \ge 2 . Let us choose a closed point P \in X of minimal degree \deg P . Consider the sequence of linear systems |nP| for n = 1, 2, \dots . By Proposition , as soon as \deg(nP) = n \cdot \deg P > 2g - 2 , the divisor nP becomes nonspecial, meaning: l(nP) = n \cdot \deg P + 1 - g We wish to find the smallest n such that l(nP) \ge 2 , ensuring the existence of a nonconstant rational function f \in L(nP) . Setting n \cdot \deg P + 1 - g \ge 2 implies that we need n \cdot \deg P \ge g + 1 . Thus, there exists an effective divisor D = nP with \deg D \le g + 1 (or slightly adjusting the point choices if the degrees are not coprime, there always exists an effective divisor D composed of closed points such that l(D) \ge 2 and \deg D \le g + 1 ). A nonconstant element f \in L(D) corresponds to a dominant morphism f: X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k . The poles of f are contained within the support of D , and the total number of poles counted with multiplicity is bounded by \deg D . By Definition , the degree of the finite morphism f is precisely the degree of this pole divisor, which is \le \deg D \le g + 1 . ◻ Proposition 1.1 (Hyperelliptic Curves). A complete nonsingular curve X over k is called hyperelliptic if g \ge 2 and there exists a finite morphism f: X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k of degree 2. If X has genus g = 2 , then its canonical divisor K defines a complete linear system |K| of degree 2 and dimension 1 that has no base points. Consequently, every curve of genus 2 is hyperelliptic. For every genus g \ge 2 , there exists a hyperelliptic curve over k . Proof. (1) Let X be a curve of genus g = 2 . By Example , the canonical divisor K has degree: \deg K = 2g - 2 = 2(2) - 2 = 2 By definition of the geometric genus, l(K) = g = 2 . Thus, the dimension of the complete linear system |K| is \dim |K| = l(K) - 1 = 1 . To show that |K| has no base points, suppose for contradiction that P \in X is a base point of |K| . This would mean that every effective divisor in |K| contains P , implying l(K - P) = l(K) = 2 . Let us apply the Riemann–Roch theorem to the divisor P : l(P) - l(K - P) = \deg P + 1 - g \implies l(P) - 2 = \deg P + 1 - 2 l(P) = \deg P + 1 However, by Proposition , since g = 2

eq 0 , we must have \dim |P| < \deg P \implies l(P) - 1 < \deg P \implies l(P) \le \deg P . This directly contradicts l(P) = \deg P + 1 . Thus, |K| has no base points. Because |K| is a base-point-free linear system of dimension 1 and degree 2, the complete linear system defines a global morphism \varphi_{|K|}: X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k . Since \deg K = 2 , the degree of this finite morphism is exactly 2. Because g = 2 \ge 2 , this satisfies the definition, proving that X is hyperelliptic. (2) To show that hyperelliptic curves exist for any genus g \ge 2 , we can generalize the construction from Remark . Consider the smooth quadric surface Q \cong \mathbb{P}^1_k 	imes \mathbb{P}^1_k \subset \mathbb{P}^3_k . A divisor class on Q is determined by its bi-degree (a, b) . Let X be an irreducible, nonsingular curve defined by a divisor of type (g+1, 2) on \mathbb{P}^1_k 	imes \mathbb{P}^1_k . The adjunction formula on the surface shows that the arithmetic genus of such a curve is: p_a(X) = (a-1)(b-1) = (g+1-1)(2-1) = g \cdot 1 = g The projection map from the product space onto the second factor, \pi_2: \mathbb{P}^1_k 	imes \mathbb{P}^1_k 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k , restricts to a morphism on our curve: f = \pi_2|_X : X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k Since the curve X has degree 2 with respect to the second projection (its bi-degree component is b=2 ), every fiber of \pi_2 intersects X at exactly 2 points (counted with multiplicity). Therefore, f: X 	o \mathbb{P}^1_k is a finite morphism of degree 2. Since g \ge 2 , this confirms that X is a hyperelliptic curve of genus g . ◻ Singular Curves and the Normalization Morphism Up to this point, our theory has heavily relied on the assumption that the curve X is nonsingular, which ensures that all local rings are discrete valuation rings and that Weil divisors correspond perfectly to invertible sheaves. We now generalize these concepts to singular curves, utilizing the normalization morphism to analyze local singularities and establishing a version of the Riemann–Roch theorem for singular projective curves. Let X be an integral projective scheme of dimension 1 over a field k (which may have singular points), and let \pi: \widetilde{X} 	o X be its normalization. The scheme \widetilde{X} is a complete nonsingular curve, and \pi is a finite birational morphism. Since \pi is an isomorphism outside a finite set of singular points, the quotient sheaf is a skyscraper sheaf supported precisely at the singular points of X . For each point P \in X , we define the local invariant \delta_P as the length of the \mathcal{O}_{X,P} -module \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_P / \mathcal{O}_P : \delta_P = \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{X,P}} (\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_P / \mathcal{O}_P) = \dim_k (\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_P / \mathcal{O}_P) Note that \delta_P = 0 if and only if P is a regular (nonsingular) point of X . title: Plane Geometry
text: OPEN FILE Classical Geometry Plane Geometry Plane Geometry Intersection Numbers We first define intersection numbers analytically via the Euler-Poincaré characteristic. This establishes a fundamentally topological and homological foundation for the theory. Definition 2.1 (Intersection Number via Euler Characteristics). Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension n . Let \mathcal{L}_1, \dots, \mathcal{L}_n be invertible sheaves on X . The intersection number of these sheaves is defined as the alternating sum of the Euler characteristics of their tensor products: (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_n) \coloneqq \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}} (-1)^{n - |I|} \chi\Big(X, \bigotimes_{i \in I} \mathcal{L}_i\Big). To demonstrate that this definition is well-behaved, we must understand the behavior of the Euler characteristic under tensor operations. This brings us to a foundational theorem which asserts that the Euler characteristic of a tensor product of powers of invertible sheaves behaves polynomially. Theorem 2.1 (Snapper’s Polynomial Theorem). Let X be a smooth projective variety, and let \mathcal{F} be a coherent sheaf on X with s = \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} . Let \mathcal{L}_1, \dots, \mathcal{L}_t be t invertible sheaves on X . Then the Euler-Poincaré characteristic \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}). is a numerical polynomial in n_1, \dots, n_t of total degree s . (By a numerical polynomial in n_1, \dots, n_t , we mean a polynomial with rational coefficients which assumes integer values whenever n_1, \dots, n_t are integers.) Proof. We proceed by induction on s , the dimension of the support of \mathcal{F} . Base Case: When s = -1 , the support is empty, meaning \mathcal{F} = 0 . The theorem holds trivially since the Euler characteristic is uniformly 0 . Inductive Step: Assume s \ge 0 . By standard dévissage arguments for coherent sheaves on projective schemes, it suffices to prove the theorem for \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_Y , where Y is an irreducible closed subvariety. Since we are focusing on the smooth projective case, we may smoothly reduce to assuming \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_X (so s = \dim X ), and we proceed by induction on t , the number of invertible sheaves. When t = 0 , the statement is trivial. Because X is smooth, its local rings are UFDs, allowing us to find a Cartier divisor D such that \mathcal{L}_1 \simeq \mathcal{O}_X(D) . We define two coherent sheaves of ideals: \mathcal{I} = \mathcal{O}_X(-D) \cap \mathcal{O}_X \quad \text{and} \quad \mathcal{J} = \mathcal{I} \cdot \mathcal{O}_X(D) \simeq \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1. From these, we construct the torsion sheaves \mathcal{S} = \mathcal{O}_X / \mathcal{I} and \mathcal{K} = (\mathcal{O}_X / \mathcal{J}) \otimes \mathcal{L}_1 . Since \mathcal{S} and \mathcal{K} are supported on proper closed subschemes of X , their support dimensions are strictly less than s . Thus, by our outer induction hypothesis on s , the theorem already holds for \mathcal{S} and \mathcal{K} . Tensoring the short exact sequences associated with \mathcal{S} and \mathcal{K} by the appropriate powers of our invertible sheaves yields two new exact sequences: 0 \to \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{S} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to 0 and 0 \to \mathcal{J} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes (n_1-1)} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes (n_1-1)} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{K} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes (n_1-2)} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to 0. Because \mathcal{J} \simeq \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1 , the first term of the second sequence is isomorphic to the first term of the first sequence. The Euler characteristic \chi is additive on short exact sequences, so we subtract the Euler characteristic of the middle term of the second sequence from that of the first sequence: \begin{align*} &\chi(\mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) - \chi(\mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes (n_1-1)} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) \\ &= \chi(\mathcal{S} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) - \chi(\mathcal{K} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes (n_1-2)} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}). \end{align*} By our induction hypothesis on s , both terms on the right-hand side are numerical polynomials in n_1, \dots, n_t of total degree less than s = \dim X . We have shown that the first difference of the function with respect to n_1 is a polynomial of degree strictly less than s . Furthermore, since \chi(\mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) is a numerical polynomial in n_2, \dots, n_t of degree s by induction on t , the theorem follows immediately from the calculus of finite differences. ◻ We now introduce an alternative, highly useful perspective on intersection numbers formulated by Snapper, which explicitly uses the coefficients of the Euler characteristic polynomial. Definition 2.2 (Intersection Number via Polynomial Coefficients). Let X be a smooth projective variety, and let \mathcal{L}_1, \dots, \mathcal{L}_t be t invertible sheaves on X ( t \ge 0 ). Let \mathcal{F} be a coherent sheaf on X such that \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} \le t . The intersection number (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) = (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F})_X is defined as the coefficient of the monomial n_1 \cdots n_t in the polynomial \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) . Before proceeding, it is necessary to rigorously establish that this coefficient definition is completely consistent with our initial definition using the alternating sum of Euler characteristics, specifically in the case where t = n = \dim X and \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_X . Proposition 2.1 (Equivalence of Intersection Number Definitions). Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension n , and let \mathcal{L}_1, \dots, \mathcal{L}_n be invertible sheaves on X . The coefficient of n_1 \cdots n_n in the polynomial P(n_1, \dots, n_n) = \chi(X, \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_n^{\otimes n_n}) is exactly the alternating sum: \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}} (-1)^{n - |I|} \chi\Big(X, \bigotimes_{i \in I} \mathcal{L}_i\Big). Proof. By Snapper’s Polynomial Theorem, P(n_1, \dots, n_n) is a polynomial of total degree at most n . Thus, we may write it as P(n_1, \dots, n_n) = C n_1 n_2 \cdots n_n + Q(n_1, \dots, n_n) , where C is the coefficient we wish to extract, and Q consists entirely of monomials of total degree at most n that strictly miss at least one variable n_k (since any monomial of degree n involving all n variables must be exactly n_1 \cdots n_n ). Consider the evaluation of the alternating sum on a general polynomial function F(n_1, \dots, n_n) . Let \mathbf{e}_I \in \{0, 1\}^n be the indicator vector of the subset I , meaning its i -th coordinate is 1 if i \in I and 0 otherwise. The alternating sum is exactly \sum_{I} (-1)^{n - |I|} F(\mathbf{e}_I) . For the target monomial F = n_1 \cdots n_n , the evaluation F(\mathbf{e}_I) is 1 if and only if I = \{1, \dots, n\} , and 0 otherwise. Thus, the alternating sum yields (-1)^0 \cdot 1 = 1 . For any monomial in Q , there is some variable n_k that does not appear. The value of this monomial on \mathbf{e}_I depends only on the coordinates in I \setminus \{k\} . We can partition the subsets of \{1, \dots, n\} into pairs (I, I \cup \{k\}) where k \notin I . For each pair, the monomial evaluates to the same number, but the signs (-1)^{n - |I|} and (-1)^{n - (|I|+1)} are opposite, causing exact cancellation. Therefore, the alternating sum annihilates Q . Applying the alternating sum to P isolates exactly the coefficient C , proving the equivalence. ◻ With consistency established, we now explore the fundamental properties of the intersection number, relying heavily on the structure of numerical polynomials. Lemma 2.1 (Basis for Numerical Polynomials). A polynomial F(n_1, \dots, n_t) is numerical if and only if it can be written in the form F(n_1, \dots, n_t) = \sum a(i_1, \dots, i_t) \binom{n_1 + i_1}{i_1} \cdots \binom{n_t + i_t}{i_t}. where the coefficients a(i_1, \dots, i_t) are integers, and i_1 \ge 0, \dots, i_t \ge 0 . Here, for all n , \binom{n+i}{i} = \frac{(n+i)(n+i-1)\cdots(n+1)}{i(i-1)\cdots 1} if i > 0 , = 1 if i = 0 , and = 0 if i < 0 . Proof. This is a standard algebraic result. The binomial coefficients \binom{n+i}{i} map integers to integers and form a \mathbb{Q} -basis for polynomials in one variable. Taking tensor products of this basis gives a basis for polynomials in t variables. The integrality of the coefficients a(i_1, \dots, i_t) is both necessary and sufficient for the polynomial to be numerical, which can be shown by straightforward induction on the degree. ◻ An obvious but important fact is that the intersection number should be an integer. Proposition 2.1 (Integrality of Intersection Numbers). The intersection number (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) is an integer. Proof. By Snapper’s Polynomial Theorem, \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) is a numerical polynomial in n_1, \dots, n_t of degree s = \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} \le t . By Lemma , it can be expanded with integer coefficients a(i_1, \dots, i_t) . The term n_1 \cdots n_t can only arise from the basis elements where i_1 = 1, \dots, i_t = 1 , since any higher index would increase the total degree beyond t , and any lower index would omit a variable. For i_j = 1 , \binom{n_j+1}{1} = n_j + 1 . Thus, the coefficient of n_1 \cdots n_t is exactly the integer a(1, \dots, 1) . ◻ If a sheaf is supported only in very few parts, it is also easy to imagine that the number of intersections with other sheaves should be zero. Proposition 2.1 (Vanishing for Small Support). (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) = 0 if \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} < t , and (\mathcal{F}) = h^0(\mathcal{F}) if \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} = t = 0 . Proof. If \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} < t , then \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) is a polynomial of total degree strictly less than t . Consequently, it cannot contain a monomial of degree t , so the coefficient of n_1 \cdots n_t is identically 0 . If \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} = t = 0 , the "empty" intersection number (\mathcal{F}) is simply the constant term of the polynomial, which is evaluated at n_i = 0 . This gives \chi(\mathcal{F}) . Since \mathcal{F} is supported on a zero-dimensional scheme, its higher cohomology vanishes, yielding \chi(\mathcal{F}) = h^0(\mathcal{F}) . ◻ The most important and essential property of the intersection number is that it is a bilinear form. This plays an important role in algebraic geometry. Proposition 2.1 (Linearity and Symmetry). (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) is a symmetric t -linear form in the variables \mathcal{L}_1, \dots, \mathcal{L}_t . Proof. Symmetry is immediate from the definition, as the tensor product of invertible sheaves is commutative, rendering the polynomial symmetric with respect to permutations of the index set. To demonstrate linearity in the first variable (and thus all variables by symmetry), let \mathcal{M} and \mathcal{N} be invertible sheaves. We evaluate the intersection number involving \mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{N}^{-1} . Consider the polynomial for the sheaves \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{N}^{-1}, \mathcal{L}_2, \dots, \mathcal{L}_t : \begin{align*} &\chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{M}^{\otimes m} \otimes (\mathcal{N}^{-1})^{\otimes n} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) \\ &= (\mathcal{M} \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) m n_2 \cdots n_t - (\mathcal{N} \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) n n_2 \cdots n_t + \cdots \end{align*} This expansion is justified by taking successively n=0 and m=0 to isolate the respective coefficients. Now, set m = n = n_1 to represent the powers of the combined sheaf \mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{N}^{-1} . Substituting this yields: \begin{align*} &\chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes (\mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{N}^{-1})^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) \\ &= \big( (\mathcal{M} \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) - (\mathcal{N} \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) \big) n_1 n_2 \cdots n_t + \cdots \end{align*} The coefficient of n_1 \cdots n_t on the left side is by definition ((\mathcal{M} \otimes \mathcal{N}^{-1}) \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) , confirming the linearity. ◻ Finally, we address the behavior of intersection numbers with respect to the sheaf argument \mathcal{F} . Proposition 2.1 (Additivity on Exact Sequences). If 0 \to \mathcal{F}' \to \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}'' \to 0 is an exact sequence of coherent sheaves, then (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) = (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}') + (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}''). Proof. Because the functor - \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} is exact (as we are tensoring with locally free sheaves), tensoring the given short exact sequence maintains exactness. The Euler-Poincaré characteristic is additive on short exact sequences, so we have the identity of polynomials: \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) = \chi(\mathcal{F}' \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) + \chi(\mathcal{F}'' \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}). Extracting the coefficient of n_1 \cdots n_t from both sides of this equation immediately yields the desiUniBlue additivity formula. Note that exactness at stalks ensures that \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} \le t if and only if both \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F}' \le t and \dim \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F}'' \le t , keeping the definition well-posed. ◻ Remark 2.1 (Notation Convention). Let W \subset X be a closed subscheme of dimension less than or equal to t , and take \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_W . For simplicity, it is common practice to write (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot W) in place of (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{O}_W) . Furthermore, if W = X , the notation is abbreviated simply to (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t) to mean (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot X) . An essential geometric computation relates the intersection number involving an invertible sheaf to the intersection number on an effective divisor linearly equivalent to that sheaf. Proposition 2.1 (Intersection with an Effective Divisor). If \Delta \in |\mathcal{L}_1| , representing the set of all effective divisors \Delta such that \mathcal{O}_X(\Delta) \simeq \mathcal{L}_1 , and \Delta \cap \operatorname{Ass} \mathcal{F} = \emptyset , then (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}) = (\mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}_\Delta). where \mathcal{F}_\Delta = \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{O}_\Delta . In particular, if \dim X \le t , then (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdot \mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t) = (\mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \Delta) . Proof. Because \Delta \cap \operatorname{Ass} \mathcal{F} = \emptyset , any local equation of the effective divisor \Delta at a point x \in X is not a zero divisor in the stalk \mathcal{F}_x . Consequently, tensoring the structural exact sequence of \Delta with \mathcal{F} and the invertible sheaves yields an exact sequence: 0 \to \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes(n_1-1)} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to \mathcal{F}_\Delta \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t} \to 0. Taking the Euler-Poincaré characteristics gives: \begin{align*} \chi(\mathcal{F}_\Delta \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) &= \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes n_1} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) - \chi(\mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes(n_1-1)} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) \\ &= (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F})n_1 \cdots n_t + \cdots - (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F})(n_1 - 1)n_2 \cdots n_t + \cdots \\ &= (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F})n_2 \cdots n_t + \cdots \end{align*} . On the other hand, evaluating the characteristic of \mathcal{F}_\Delta explicitly at n_1 = 0 provides: \chi(\mathcal{F}_\Delta \otimes \mathcal{L}_1^{\otimes 0} \otimes \mathcal{L}_2^{\otimes n_2} \cdots \otimes \mathcal{L}_t^{\otimes n_t}) = (\mathcal{L}_2 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F}_\Delta)n_2 \cdots n_t + \cdots. Comparing the coefficients of the monomial n_2 \cdots n_t from both approaches confirms the proposition. ◻ Proposition 2.1 (Restriction to Subschemes). Suppose we have the incidence of closed subschemes Y \subset W \subset X , where Y = \operatorname{supp}\mathcal{F} . Then (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot \mathcal{F})_X = (\mathcal{L}_{1|W} \cdots \mathcal{L}_{t|W} \cdot \mathcal{F})_W. In particular, (\mathcal{L}_1 \cdots \mathcal{L}_t \cdot W)_X = (\mathcal{L}_{1|W} \cdots \mathcal{L}_{t|W})_W . Proof. Because Y is the support of \mathcal{F} , \mathcal{F} may be consideUniBlue an \mathcal{O}_W -module for any W containing Y . Let X,Y\subset\mathbb{P}^n_k be pure-dimensional closed subschemes of codimensions p and q , respectively. Assume p+q\leq n and that X and Y intersect properly, i.e. every irreducible component W\subset X\cap Y has codimension \operatorname{codim}_{\mathbb{P}^n}W=p+q. Then \begin{equation} \boxed{ \deg(X\cdot Y) = \deg(X)\deg(Y) }. \end{equation} More explicitly, the proper intersection cycle is \begin{equation} X\cdot Y = \sum_{W\in\mathrm{Irr}(X\cap Y)} i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)[W], \end{equation} and hence \begin{equation} \boxed{ \sum_{W\in\mathrm{Irr}(X\cap Y)} i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)\deg W = \deg X\deg Y. } \end{equation} Here i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n) denotes the local intersection multiplicity of X and Y along W . Proof. Since \mathbb{P}^n is smooth, its Chow groups carry an intersection product \operatorname{CH}^p(\mathbb{P}^n)\times\operatorname{CH}^q(\mathbb{P}^n) \longrightarrow \operatorname{CH}^{p+q}(\mathbb{P}^n). Put a=\deg X, \qquad b=\deg Y. By Lemma , [X]=ah^p and [Y]=bh^q. Therefore \begin{align} [X]\cdot[Y] &= (ah^p)(bh^q)\notag\\ &= ab\,h^{p+q}. \end{align} Because X and Y meet properly, the intersection product is represented by the proper intersection cycle X\cdot Y = \sum_W i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)[W], where W runs through the irreducible components of X\cap Y . Every such W has dimension \dim W = n-p-q. Set d=n-p-q. To compute the degree of the intersection cycle, multiply by h^d . We obtain \begin{align*} [X]\cdot[Y]\cdot h^d &= ab\,h^{p+q+d}\\ &= ab\,h^n. \end{align*} Taking degrees and using \deg(h^n)=1 gives \deg(X\cdot Y) = ab = \deg X\deg Y. This proves . On the other hand, by linearity of the degree map, \begin{align*} \deg(X\cdot Y) &= \deg \left( \sum_W i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)[W] \right)\\ &= \sum_W i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)\deg W. \end{align*} Combining this with \deg(X\cdot Y) = \deg X\deg Y gives \sum_W i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n)\deg W = \deg X\deg Y. This is . ◻ Remark 2.1 (Local intersection multiplicity). Because \mathbb{P}^n is nonsingular, the local ring \mathcal O_{\mathbb{P}^n,\eta_W} at the generic point \eta_W of an irreducible component W is a regular local ring. Under the proper-intersection hypothesis, the intersection multiplicity may be expressed by Serre’s formula \begin{equation} i(W;X,Y;\mathbb{P}^n) = \sum_{j\geq0} (-1)^j \mathrm{length}_{\mathcal O_{\mathbb{P}^n,\eta_W}} \mathrm{Tor}_j^{\mathcal O_{\mathbb{P}^n,\eta_W}} \left( \mathcal O_{X,\eta_W}, \mathcal O_{Y,\eta_W} \right). \end{equation}

text: OPEN FILE Classical Geometry Weil Conjectures on Curves Weil Conjectures on Curves What are Weil Conjectures? To understand the profound impact of the Weil Conjectures, we must trace their origins through the history of number theory and algebraic geometry, beginning with a striking analogy between numbers and polynomials. Remark 3.1 (Historical Context: From Artin to Hasse). In 1924, Emil Artin observed a deep structural similarity between algebraic number fields (such as \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D}) ) and function fields over finite fields (such as \mathbb{F}_p(x, \sqrt{f(x)}) ). Just as the classic Riemann \zeta -function studies the distribution of prime numbers over the ring of integers \mathbb{Z} , Artin defined a \zeta -function for the polynomial ring \mathbb{F}_q[x] : \zeta(s) = \sum_{A} \frac{1}{|A|^s} = \prod_{P} \left(1 - \frac{1}{|P|^s}\right)^{-1}. where A runs over all monic polynomials and P runs over all irreducible monic polynomials. Following this analogy, Helmut Hasse (between 1933 and 1936) utilized the theory of complex multiplication to solve the Riemann Hypothesis for algebraic curves of genus g=1 (elliptic curves). By estimating the zeroes of the \zeta -function, Hasse proved the famous bound for the number of rational points N on an elliptic curve over \mathbb{F}_q : |N - (q + 1)| \le 2\sqrt{q}. Between 1940 and 1941, while incarcerated in a military prison in Rouen, France, André Weil sought to generalize Hasse’s work from elliptic curves to smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curves of arbitrary genus g . Weil realized that the classical Italian school of algebraic geometry lacked the rigorous foundations necessary to handle spaces over fields of positive characteristic. Consequently, he spent the following years completely rebuilding algebraic geometry using the language of abstract algebra, culminating in his treatises Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (1946) and Sur les courbes algébriques (1948). By 1949, after studying Gauss and Jacobi sums and counting points on diagonal hypersurfaces, Weil discovered that the patterns governing rational points on curves were not isolated phenomena. They were manifestations of a profound topological structure shaUniBlue by algebraic varieties of all dimensions. He formally proposed this in his landmark paper Numbers of solutions of equations in finite fields , giving birth to the classic Weil Conjectures. To state the conjectures, we first define the generating function that encodes the number of solutions to a system of polynomial equations over extensions of a finite field. Definition 3.1 (The Local Zeta Function). Let X be an n -dimensional smooth projective algebraic variety defined over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q . Let N_m denote the number of rational points of X over the degree- m extension field \mathbb{F}_{q^m} (i.e., N_m = |X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})| ). The local zeta function of X is defined as the formal power series: Z(X, t) = \exp\left( \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{N_m}{m} t^m \right). The Weil Conjectures state that this power series, constructed purely from combinatorial counting, exhibits extraordinary analytic and topological properties. Theorem 3.1 (The Weil Conjectures (1949)). Let X be an n -dimensional smooth projective variety over \mathbb{F}_q . The zeta function Z(X, t) satisfies the following four properties: Rationality: Z(X, t) is a rational function in t . That is, there exist polynomials P(t), Q(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[t] such that Z(X, t) = \frac{P(t)}{Q(t)} . Functional Equation: Let \chi be the Euler characteristic of X . The zeta function satisfies a highly symmetric functional equation linking the values at t and 1/(q^n t) : Z\left(X, \frac{1}{q^n t}\right) = \pm q^{\frac{n\chi}{2}} t^\chi Z(X, t). Riemann Hypothesis: This is the deepest part of the conjecture. The rational function factors into an alternating product of polynomials: Z(X, t) = \frac{P_1(t) P_3(t) \cdots P_{2n-1}(t)}{P_0(t) P_2(t) \cdots P_{2n}(t)}. where each P_i(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t] . Furthermore: P_0(t) = 1 - t P_{2n}(t) = 1 - q^n t For 1 \le i \le 2n-1 , every root \alpha of P_i(t) has absolute value |\alpha| = q^{-i/2} in the complex plane. (Substituting t = q^{-s} places the zeroes on the critical line \operatorname{Re}(s) = i/2 ). Betti Numbers: If X is obtained by the good reduction modulo p of a smooth projective variety \mathcal{X} defined over a number field K \subset \mathbb{C} , then the degree of P_i(t) is equal to the i -th topological Betti number of the complex manifold \mathcal{X}(\mathbb{C}) : \deg P_i(t) = \beta_i(\mathcal{X}(\mathbb{C})). To truly appreciate the power of these conjectures, let us specialize to the case of a curve, which is the core object of our current study. Let X be a smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve over \mathbb{F}_q . Because a curve has dimension n = 1 , the Betti number sequence for a corresponding compact Riemann surface of genus g is \beta_0 = 1 , \beta_1 = 2g , and \beta_2 = 1 . The Weil Conjectures drastically simplify this scenario. Corollary 3.1 (Weil Conjectures for Curves). For a smooth projective curve X of genus g over \mathbb{F}_q , the polynomials P_i(t) vanish for i > 2 . The zeta function takes the precise form: Z(X, t) = \frac{P_1(t)}{(1-t)(1-qt)}. where P_1(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t] is a polynomial of degree 2g . The roots of P_1(t) can be written as \alpha_1^{-1}, \dots, \alpha_{2g}^{-1} , where each algebraic integer \alpha_j has complex absolute value |\alpha_j| = \sqrt{q} . Remark 3.1 (Why this matters: The Point-Counting Formula). The true magic of the Riemann Hypothesis for curves reveals itself when we extract the point counts N_m . By taking the logarithmic derivative of Z(X, t) = \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{2g} (1 - \alpha_j t)}{(1-t)(1-qt)} and comparing coefficients with the original definition \exp(\sum \frac{N_m}{m} t^m) , we obtain a breathtakingly exact formula for the number of points: N_m = q^m + 1 - \sum_{j=1}^{2g} \alpha_j^m. Because we know the absolute value of every \alpha_j is \sqrt{q} , we can apply the triangle inequality to instantly derive the generalized Hasse-Weil Bound for a curve of arbitrary genus g : |N_m - (q^m + 1)| \le 2g q^{m/2}. This tells us that the number of points on a curve over a finite field is approximately q^m + 1 , with an error term tightly constrained by the geometry (the genus g ) of the curve! To rigorously define the point-counting numbers N_m = |X(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})| used in the Weil Conjectures, we must define what a “point” over a field extension means in the language of scheme theory, and how the Galois group acts upon these points. Definition 3.2 ( K -Rational Points). Let X be a scheme over a field k , and let K be a field extension of k . The set of K -rational points of X , denoted X(K) , is defined as the set of k -morphisms from \operatorname{Spec}K to X : X(K) = \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}K, X). Every individual morphism P \colon \operatorname{Spec}K \to X is referUniBlue to as a K -point of X . Definition 3.3 (Galois Action on Points). Let K/k be a Galois field extension with Galois group G = \operatorname{Gal}(K/k) . For any automorphism \sigma \in G and any K -point P \in X(K) , the action of \sigma on P is defined by the composition of morphisms: \sigma \cdot P := P \circ \operatorname{Spec}(\sigma^{-1}). where \operatorname{Spec}(\sigma^{-1}) \colon \operatorname{Spec}K \to \operatorname{Spec}K is the scheme morphism canonically induced by the field automorphism \sigma^{-1} \colon K \to K . To compute with K -points, it is highly practical to relate these abstract morphisms back to the underlying topological space of the scheme X . Proposition 3.1 (Characterization of Rational Points). Let X be a k -scheme and let k' be a field extension of k . The k' -rational points of X (the elements f \in \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}k', X) ) are in canonical bijection with pairs (x, \iota) , where x \in X is a point in the underlying topological space of X , and \iota \colon \kappa(x) \hookrightarrow k' is a k -linear field embedding of the residue field \kappa(x) into k' . Proof. Let f \in \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}k', X) be a given morphism. The underlying topological space of \operatorname{Spec}k' is a single point, denoted * . The continuous map on topological spaces must send * to some specific point x \in X , so f(*) = x . At the level of structure sheaves, the morphism f induces a homomorphism of local rings at the target point: f^\sharp _x \colon \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \to k'. Because f is a morphism of locally ringed spaces, f^\sharp _x is a local ring homomorphism. This strictly means the maximal ideal \mathfrak{m}_x of \mathcal{O}_{X,x} must be mapped into the unique maximal ideal of the field k' , which is simply the zero ideal (0) . Therefore, the kernel of f^\sharp _x contains \mathfrak{m}_x , and the homomorphism naturally factors through the quotient: \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{O}_{X,x}/\mathfrak{m}_x = \kappa(x) \hookrightarrow k'. This canonical injection \kappa(x) \hookrightarrow k' provides our embedding \iota . Conversely, suppose we are given a topological point x \in X and a k -linear embedding \iota \colon \kappa(x) \hookrightarrow k' . For any affine open set U \subseteq X containing x , we have a natural composite ring homomorphism: \mathcal{O}_X(U) \to \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \twoheadrightarrow \kappa(x) \xrightarrow{\iota} k'. Taking the spectrum of this ring homomorphism constructs a unique scheme morphism \operatorname{Spec}k' \to U \hookrightarrow X , which precisely yields the k' -point f . ◻ Corollary 3.1 (). When k' = k , the k -rational points X(k) correspond strictly bijectively to the closed points x \in X that satisfy the residue field condition \kappa(x) = k . When we study the points of X over an algebraic closure, the Galois group groups these points into distinct orbits. The size of these orbits depends entirely on the degree of the residue fields of the closed points of X . Proposition 3.1 (Fibers and Galois Orbits). Let \bar{k} be an algebraic closure of a perfect field k , and let \pi \colon \bar{X} = X \times_k \bar{k} \to X be the natural projection morphism. For any closed point x \in X , its geometric fiber \bar{X}_x = \pi^{-1}(x) satisfies: \#\bar{X}_x = [\kappa(x) : k]. Furthermore, the absolute Galois group G = \operatorname{Gal}(\bar{k}/k) acts transitively on the points of \bar{X}_x ; that is, \bar{X}_x constitutes a single Galois orbit under the action of G . Proof. By the definition of the scheme-theoretic fiber, the fiber over x is isomorphic to the base change of its residue field: \bar{X}_x \simeq \operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(x) \otimes_k \bar{k}). Because k is perfect, the finite field extension \kappa(x)/k is a separable extension. By the Primitive Element Theorem, \kappa(x) is generated by a single element, so \kappa(x) \simeq k[z]/(f(z)) for some irreducible separable polynomial f(z) \in k[z] . We can then compute the tensor product explicitly: \kappa(x) \otimes_k \bar{k} \simeq \left( k[z]/(f(z)) \right) \otimes_k \bar{k} \simeq \bar{k}[z]/(f(z)). Since \bar{k} is an algebraically closed field, the polynomial f(z) splits completely into distinct linear factors over \bar{k} , yielding roots \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n \in \bar{k} , where n = \deg(f) = [\kappa(x) : k] . Applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem to the pairwise coprime ideals (z - \alpha_i) , the ring decomposes into a direct product: \bar{k}[z]/(f(z)) \simeq \prod_{i=1}^n \bar{k}[z]/(z - \alpha_i) \simeq \prod_{i=1}^n \bar{k}. Taking the spectrum transforms this direct product of rings into a disjoint union of schemes: \bar{X}_x \simeq \operatorname{Spec}\left( \prod_{i=1}^n \bar{k} \right) \simeq \coprod_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}. This shows that the fiber consists of exactly n distinct points, proving that \#\bar{X}_x = \deg(f) = [\kappa(x) : k] . Finally, we consider the Galois action. Because f(z) is an irreducible polynomial over k , classical Galois theory states that the absolute Galois group G = \operatorname{Gal}(\bar{k}/k) acts transitively on the set of its roots \{\alpha_i\} . Since the geometric points of the fiber \bar{X}_x correspond exactly to these roots, the Galois group G acts transitively on the n points of the fiber. Therefore, the geometric points lying over a single closed point x \in X form exactly one complete Galois orbit. ◻ The proof of the First Part To translate the geometric problem of point-counting into algebraic machinery, we must fix our base field and study the divisors on our curve. Let k = \mathbb{F}_q be a finite field with q elements. Throughout this section, let X be a smooth, projective, and geometrically irreducible curve over k of genus g . In the language of schemes, we formulate the specific objects that construct the Weil Conjectures as follows: For any closed point x \in |X| (where |X| denotes the underlying topological space of the scheme X ), the degree of x is defined as the degree of its residue field over the base field: \deg(x) = [\kappa(x) : k] . An effective Weil divisor on X is a formal sum D = \sum_{x \in |X|} n_x x , where the coefficients n_x are non-negative integers ( n_x \ge 0 ) and only finitely many n_x are strictly positive. The degree of the divisor extends the degree of points linearly: \deg(D) = \sum_{x \in |X|} n_x \deg(x) . The set of all effective divisors is denoted \operatorname{Div}^+(X) . Let k_s = \mathbb{F}_{q^s} be the unique field extension of k of degree s . The set of k_s -rational points on X is denoted X(k_s) = \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}k_s, X) . To construct the Zeta function combinatorially, we define three sequences of non-negative integers indexed by s \ge 1 (with A_0 = 1 by convention for the zero divisor): \begin{align*} A_s &= \#\{D \in \operatorname{Div}^+(X) \mid \deg(D) = s\} && \text{(Number of effective divisors of degree } s \text{)} \\ M_s &= \#\{x \in |X| \mid \deg(x) = s\} && \text{(Number of closed points of degree } s \text{)} \\ N_s &= \#X(k_s) && \text{(Number of } k_s \text{-rational points)} \end{align*} Theorem 3.1 (Equivalent Expressions of the Zeta Function). For a curve X over a finite field k = \mathbb{F}_q , the following three formal power series in the formal variable t are absolutely identical: \displaystyle \sum_{s=0}^\infty A_s t^s \displaystyle \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_s} \displaystyle \exp\left( \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{N_s}{s} t^s \right) We formally define this identical series as the local Zeta function of the curve X , denoted Z(X, t) . Proof. Proof that = : The set of effective divisors \operatorname{Div}^+(X) forms a free commutative monoid generated strictly by the closed points x \in |X| . Because of this unique factorization property (every effective divisor is a unique finite sum of closed points), we can rewrite the sum over all effective divisors as an Euler product over all closed points: \sum_{s=0}^\infty A_s t^s = \sum_{D \in \operatorname{Div}^+(X)} t^{\deg(D)} = \prod_{x \in |X|} \left( \sum_{n=0}^\infty t^{n \deg(x)} \right). By evaluating the inner geometric series for each point x , this becomes: \prod_{x \in |X|} (1 - t^{\deg(x)})^{-1}. We can now group the terms in this infinite product by the degree of the closed points. Let s = \deg(x) . By definition, there are exactly M_s closed points of degree s . Grouping these identical factors together yields: \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_s}. This proves that and are equivalent. Proof that = : By Proposition , specifying a k_s -rational point is perfectly equivalent to choosing a closed point x \in |X| alongside a k -linear field embedding of its residue field into the target field: \kappa(x) \hookrightarrow k_s . Such an embedding exists if and only if the degree d = \deg(x) = [\kappa(x):k] divides the extension degree s . Furthermore, standard Galois theory of finite fields dictates that if one such embedding exists, there are exactly d distinct embeddings, corresponding to the conjugates under the action of \operatorname{Gal}(\kappa(x)/k) . Therefore, if we classify the rational points by the degree d of their underlying closed point, we obtain the fundamental counting formula: N_s = \sum_{d \mid s} d M_d. Now, we apply the formal logarithm to the infinite product in . Using the Taylor expansion \log(1-X) = -\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{X^k}{k} , we obtain: \begin{align*} \log \left( \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_s} \right) &= -\sum_{d=1}^\infty M_d \log(1 - t^d) \\ &= \sum_{d=1}^\infty M_d \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{dk}}{k} \end{align*} To re-index this double sum, let s = dk . Then k = s/d . For a fixed s \ge 1 , the inner sum will iterate over all divisors d of s . Substituting k gives: \begin{align*} \sum_{d=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty M_d \frac{t^{dk}}{k} &= \sum_{s=1}^\infty \left( \sum_{d \mid s} M_d \frac{d}{s} \right) t^s \\ &= \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{1}{s} \left( \sum_{d \mid s} d M_d \right) t^s \\ &= \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{N_s}{s} t^s \end{align*} Taking the formal exponential \exp of both sides immediately shows that the product equals the exponential generating function . This concludes the proof of the theorem. ◻ To prove the rationality of Z(X, t) , we will eventually group the effective divisors D not just by their degree, but by their linear equivalence classes. We must therefore count how many effective divisors exist in a given linear equivalence class. Theorem 3.1 (Size of a Complete Linear System). Let D be a divisor on the curve X , and let \ell(D) = \dim_k \operatorname{H}^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D)) . Assuming \ell(D) > 0 , the number of effective divisors that are linearly equivalent to D (i.e., the cardinality of the complete linear system |D| ) is exactly: \frac{q^{\ell(D)} - 1}{q - 1}. Proof. Because X is a geometrically irreducible projective scheme over k , the ring of global regular functions is simply the base field itself: \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = k . Consequently, the group of globally invertible regular functions is the multiplicative group of the field: \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X^\times) = k^\times . There is a canonical bijection between the effective divisors in the complete linear system |D| and the non-zero global sections of the line bundle \mathcal{O}_X(D) modulo scaling by global invertible functions. That is: |D| \longleftrightarrow \left( \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D)) \setminus \{0\} \right) / k^\times. The space of global sections \Gamma(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D)) is a k -vector space of dimension \ell(D) . Since the base field has q elements, this vector space contains exactly q^{\ell(D)} total elements. Removing the zero section leaves q^{\ell(D)} - 1 non-zero sections. The group k^\times acts on these non-zero sections by scalar multiplication. Because X is an integral scheme, the space of sections is torsion-free, meaning the multiplication action by any element of k^\times (other than 1 ) has no fixed points on the non-zero sections. Thus, the action is free. Since the group k^\times has order q - 1 , each orbit under this action has exactly q - 1 elements. The number of orbits, which corresponds exactly to the number of effective divisors in |D| , is the total number of non-zero sections divided by the size of the orbits: \#|D| = \frac{q^{\ell(D)} - 1}{q - 1}. Geometrically, this demonstrates that over a finite field, the complete linear system |D| is simply the set of rational points of the projective space \mathbb{P}^{\ell(D)-1}(\mathbb{F}_q) . ◻ Lemma 3.1 (Finiteness of Effective Divisors of Bounded Degree). For any integer d \ge 0 , the set of effective divisors of degree d on X is finite. That is, the set \operatorname{Div}_+^d(X) := \{E \in \operatorname{Div}(X) \mid E \ge 0, \deg(E) = d\}. is a finite set. Proof. An effective divisor can be uniquely represented as a formal sum E = \sum n_x x , where x \in |X| are closed points, n_x \ge 0 , and the degree satisfies \sum n_x \deg(x) = d . Because the degree of any closed point is positive ( \deg(x) \ge 1 ), the points x actively participating in this sum (where n_x > 0 ) must individually satisfy \deg(x) \le d . Because X is a projective scheme over k , it admits a closed immersion into some projective space \mathbb{P}^n_k . For any closed point x \in |X| with \deg(x) = r \le d , its residue field \kappa(x) is isomorphic to the finite field \mathbb{F}_{q^r} . This structure gives rise to a naturally defined morphism \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{F}_{q^r} \to X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^n_k , which corresponds to a specific rational point in \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}) . Since a projective space over a finite field only has a finite number of rational points, the set \mathbb{P}^n(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}) is finite. Consequently, its closed subset X(\mathbb{F}_{q^r}) is also finite. This implies that the total number of closed points on X whose degree does not exceed d is strictly finite. Since there are only finitely many closed points available to form the divisor E , and their respective coefficients n_x are strictly bounded by the condition \sum n_x \deg(x) = d , there are only finitely many valid linear combinations. Thus, \operatorname{Div}_+^d(X) is a finite set. ◻ Theorem 3.1 (Finiteness of \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) and the Class Number). For any integer d , the set of divisor classes of degree d , denoted \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) , is a finite set. In particular, the degree-zero Picard group \operatorname{Pic}^0(X) is a finite Abelian group. Its cardinality is called the class number of the curve X , denoted by h . Proof. We first prove that \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) is finite for any d \ge 2g . Take an arbitrary divisor class [D] \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) with d \ge 2g . By the Riemann-Roch theorem, we must consider the canonical divisor K , which has degree \deg(K) = 2g - 2 . We evaluate the degree of K - D : \deg(K - D) = 2g - 2 - d < 0. Because a divisor of negative degree cannot be linearly equivalent to an effective divisor, the space of global sections for K-D is trivial, meaning \ell(K - D) = 0 . Therefore, the Riemann-Roch formula simplifies exactly to: \ell(D) = \deg(D) + 1 - g = d + 1 - g. Since d \ge 2g , it immediately follows that \ell(D) \ge g + 1 \ge 1 . This proves that \ell(D) > 0 , meaning the complete linear system |D| is non-empty. This establishes a crucial fact: when d \ge 2g , every divisor class in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) contains at least one effective divisor. In other words, the natural quotient map mapping effective divisors to their linear equivalence class: \operatorname{Div}_+^d(X) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}^d(X). is surjective. By Lemma , the domain \operatorname{Div}_+^d(X) is a finite set. The surjective image of a finite set is necessarily finite, so \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) must be finite for d \ge 2g . Now consider an arbitrary degree r . Because the degrees of closed points on X are strictly positive, we can simply pick a sufficiently large number of closed points to construct an effective divisor D_h such that r + \deg(D_h) \ge 2g . Translation by D_h induces a group isomorphism: \operatorname{Pic}^r(X) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Pic}^{r + \deg(D_h)}(X), \quad [D] \mapsto [D + D_h]. Because the target set \operatorname{Pic}^{r + \deg(D_h)}(X) has a degree greater than or equal to 2g , we know it is finite. The bijection implies the source set \operatorname{Pic}^r(X) is also finite. Setting r=0 demonstrates that \operatorname{Pic}^0(X) is a finite group, allowing us to formally define the class number h = \#\operatorname{Pic}^0(X) . ◻ We continue to fix X as a smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve over the finite field k = \mathbb{F}_q , with genus g and class number h . Let A_s denote the number of effective divisors of degree s . Lemma 3.1 (The Greatest Common Divisor of Divisor Degrees). Let m be the greatest common divisor of the degrees of all closed points on X (equivalently, m is the smallest positive integer such that there exists a divisor of degree m on X ). Then m = 1 . Proof. We begin by observing the explicit distribution of the sequence A_s : If m \nmid s , there are strictly no divisors of degree s on X (as all degrees are multiples of m ). Thus, A_s = 0 . If m \mid s and s > 2g - 2 , the set \operatorname{Pic}^s(X) is a principal homogeneous space over \operatorname{Pic}^0(X) , meaning it contains exactly h distinct divisor classes. For each class [D] \in \operatorname{Pic}^s(X) , since s > 2g - 2 , the Riemann-Roch theorem dictates \ell(D) = s - g + 1 . By Theorem , each of the h classes contains exactly \frac{q^{s-g+1}-1}{q-1} effective divisors. Summing these up yields: A_s = h \frac{q^{s-g+1} - 1}{q - 1}. Using these two rules, we can expand the formal series of the Zeta function and re-index it using the variable t^m : \begin{align*} Z(X, t) &= \sum_{s=0}^\infty A_s t^s = \sum_{r=0}^\infty A_{rm} t^{rm} \\ &= \sum_{rm \le 2g-2} A_{rm} t^{rm} + \frac{h}{q-1} \sum_{rm > 2g-2} \left( q^{rm-g+1} - 1 \right) t^{rm} \end{align*} The first summation is simply a polynomial in t^m . The second summation is the difference of two geometric series, which can be evaluated explicitly: Z(X, t) = \left( \text{Polynomial in } t^m \right) + \frac{h}{q-1} \left( \frac{q^{1-g} (qt)^{r_0 m}}{1 - q^m t^m} - \frac{t^{r_0 m}}{1 - t^m} \right). where r_0 is the smallest integer such that r_0 m > 2g - 2 . This explicit formula shows that Z(X, t) is a rational function, a quotient of two polynomials in the variable t^m . If we view Z(X, t) as a meromorphic function on the complex plane \mathbb{C} , the presence of the term \frac{1}{1 - t^m} (whose numerator coefficient is non-zero) forces Z(X, t) to have a simple (first-order) pole at t = 1 . Now, let M_j be the number of closed points of degree j on X . Because M_j = 0 whenever m \nmid j , we can rewrite the Euler product formula of the Zeta function strictly in terms of multiples of m : Z(X, t) = \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^{ms})^{-M_{ms}}. Define an auxiliary power series f(t) = \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_{ms}} , so that the relationship is exactly Z(X, t) = f(t^m) . Since we established that Z(X, t) has a simple pole at t = 1 , it immediately follows that f(t) itself must have a simple pole at t = 1 . We now employ a base change argument. Let k_m = \mathbb{F}_{q^m} , and consider the base-changed curve X_{k_m} = X \times_k k_m . Let its Zeta function be denoted Z(X_{k_m}, t) = \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_s^*} . For any closed point x on X , its degree [\kappa(x) : k] must be a multiple of m . This implies its residue field \kappa(x) contains the subfield k_m . Thus, the field extension degrees satisfy the tower law: [\kappa(x) : k] = m \cdot [\kappa(x) : k_m] . Geometrically, this implies that a single closed point on X of degree ms , upon base change to k_m , splits completely into exactly m distinct closed points, each of degree s . This gives us a direct counting correspondence: M_s^* = m \cdot M_{ms}. Substitute this correspondence back into the Euler product for X_{k_m} : Z(X_{k_m}, t) = \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-m M_{ms}} = \left( \prod_{s=1}^\infty (1 - t^s)^{-M_{ms}} \right)^m = f(t)^m. On the other hand, X_{k_m} is itself a smooth, geometrically irreducible curve defined over the finite field k_m . The greatest common divisor of its closed point degrees is naturally 1 (as we factoUniBlue out m ). Applying the exact same analytic derivation we used for X to the curve X_{k_m} , we conclude that Z(X_{k_m}, t) as a whole must have a simple pole at t = 1 . However, we just proved that Z(X_{k_m}, t) = f(t)^m . Since f(t) has a simple pole at t=1 , the function f(t)^m inherently has a pole of order m at t=1 . To avoid a mathematical contradiction between having a simple pole and a pole of order m , it is strictly necessary that m = 1 . ◻ Theorem 3.1 (Rationality of the Zeta Function). Let X be a smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve of genus g over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q . The local Zeta function of X is a rational function of the specific form: Z(X, t) = \frac{P(t)}{(1 - t)(1 - qt)}. where P(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t] is a polynomial with integer coefficients satisfying P(0) = 1 and \deg P(t) = 2g . Furthermore, the leading term of P(t) is exactly q^g t^{2g} . Consequently, P(t) factors over the complex numbers as \prod_{i=1}^{2g} (1 - \alpha_i t) , where the reciprocal roots \alpha_i are algebraic integers. Proof. We first address the special case where g = 0 . For a curve of genus zero, the Riemann-Roch theorem simplifies significantly. For any divisor D of degree s \ge 0 , we have: \ell(D) = s + 1 - g = s + 1. Therefore, by Theorem , every divisor class of degree s contains exactly \frac{q^{s+1} - 1}{q - 1} effective divisors. Since m=1 (Lemma ), there are exactly h divisor classes of degree s . Summing over all classes yields the total number of effective divisors of degree s : A_s = h \left( \frac{q^{s+1} - 1}{q - 1} \right), \quad \forall s \ge 0. Taking s = 0 , the only effective divisor of degree zero is the zero divisor itself, so A_0 = 1 . This immediately forces the class number h = A_0 = 1 . The Zeta function then becomes a direct evaluation of geometric series: Z(X, t) = \sum_{s=0}^\infty \left( \frac{q^{s+1} - 1}{q - 1} \right) t^s = \frac{1}{q-1} \left( q \sum_{s=0}^\infty (qt)^s - \sum_{s=0}^\infty t^s \right). Z(X, t) = \frac{1}{q-1} \left( \frac{q}{1 - qt} - \frac{1}{1 - t} \right) = \frac{1}{(1 - t)(1 - qt)}. This perfectly matches the theorem’s claim with P(t) = 1 , which satisfies \deg P(t) = 2(0) = 0 and P(0) = 1 . For the general case where g \ge 1 , we already established that m=1 , meaning \operatorname{Pic}^s(X) always contains exactly h divisor classes for any integer s . By the Riemann-Roch theorem, when s > 2g - 2 , any divisor D of degree s satisfies \ell(K - D) = 0 , which dictates that \ell(D) = s - g + 1 . Thus, every class of degree s contains identically \frac{q^{s-g+1} - 1}{q - 1} effective divisors. Summing over the h classes gives the exact count for s > 2g - 2 : A_s = h \frac{q^{s-g+1} - 1}{q - 1}. To leverage this stable asymptotic behavior, we define an “expected” number of effective divisors for all s \ge 0 : A_s^* = \frac{h}{q-1} (q^{s-g+1} - 1). We can then split the full Zeta function series into a finite polynomial part (the deviations from the expected count) and a pUniBlueictable infinite series part: Z(X, t) = \sum_{s=0}^{2g-2} (A_s - A_s^*) t^s + \sum_{s=0}^\infty A_s^* t^s. We explicitly compute the infinite sum of geometric series on the right: \begin{align*} \sum_{s=0}^\infty A_s^* t^s &= \frac{h}{q-1} \sum_{s=0}^\infty \left( q^{1-g}(qt)^s - t^s \right) \\ &= \frac{h}{q-1} \left( \frac{q^{1-g}}{1 - qt} - \frac{1}{1 - t} \right) \end{align*} The left-hand sum is a finite polynomial, which we will define as Q(t) = \sum_{s=0}^{2g-2} (A_s - A_s^*) t^s . Substituting this back yields: Z(X, t) = Q(t) + \frac{h}{q-1} \left( \frac{q^{1-g}}{1 - qt} - \frac{1}{1 - t} \right). By finding a common denominator, we obtain: Z(X, t) = \frac{Q(t)(1 - t)(1 - qt) + \frac{h}{q-1} \left( q^{1-g}(1-t) - (1-qt) \right)}{(1 - t)(1 - qt)}. This proves that Z(X, t) is a rational function with the denominator (1-t)(1-qt) . Let its numerator be denoted P(t) . Because the original power series definition dictates Z(X, 0) = A_0 = 1 , evaluating the rational function at t=0 forces P(0) = 1 . It remains to compute the highest degree term of P(t) . Since the correction term in the numerator has degree at most 1, the leading term of P(t) is entirely determined by the leading term of Q(t)(1-t)(1-qt) . We must therefore find the highest degree term of Q(t) . We look at the coefficient at s = 2g - 2 . In \operatorname{Pic}^{2g-2}(X) , there are exactly h divisor classes. Exactly one of these is the canonical divisor class [K] . For [K] , the dimension of global sections is \ell(K) = g . Thus, the canonical class contains \frac{q^g - 1}{q - 1} effective divisors. For the remaining h - 1 divisor classes [D] \neq [K] of degree 2g-2 , the fact that D \not\sim K forces \ell(K - D) = 0 . Using Riemann-Roch, \ell(D) = (2g - 2) + 1 - g = g - 1 . Each of these h-1 classes contains \frac{q^{g-1} - 1}{q - 1} effective divisors. Summing these contributions gives the true exact count A_{2g-2} : \begin{align*} A_{2g-2} &= \frac{q^g - 1}{q - 1} + (h - 1)\frac{q^{g-1} - 1}{q - 1} \\ &= h \frac{q^{g-1} - 1}{q - 1} + \frac{q^g - q^{g-1}}{q - 1} \\ &= A_{2g-2}^* + q^{g-1} \end{align*} This reveals that the deviation exactly at s = 2g-2 is A_{2g-2} - A_{2g-2}^* = q^{g-1} \neq 0 . Because all terms s > 2g-2 have identically zero deviation, the polynomial Q(t) has exactly degree 2g-2 , and its leading term is precisely q^{g-1} t^{2g-2} . We now substitute this back into the structural expression for P(t) : P(t) = Q(t)(1 - t)(1 - qt) + (\text{lower degree terms}). Expanding the leading terms: \left( q^{g-1} t^{2g-2} \right) \cdot (-t) \cdot (-qt) = q^g t^{2g}. This decisively proves that \deg P(t) = 2g , and its leading term is q^g t^{2g} . Finally, because P(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t] and its constant term is P(0) = 1 , the reciprocal polynomial t^{2g} P(1/t) is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. The roots of this monic polynomial are precisely \alpha_i . Because they are roots of a monic polynomial in \mathbb{Z}[t] , the numbers \alpha_i are by definition algebraic integers. ◻ To establish the functional equation, it is highly convenient to rewrite our rational Zeta function using a slightly different algebraic grouping. Recall that the number of effective divisors in any divisor class C is exactly \frac{q^{\ell(C)} - 1}{q - 1} . If we define a new summation notation L_d = \sum_{C \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X)} q^{\ell(C)} , then the total number of effective divisors of degree d is A_d = \frac{L_d - h}{q - 1} . Substituting this into our power series naturally rearranges the Zeta function into the following compact form: Z(X, t) = \frac{1}{q-1} \left( \sum_{d=0}^{2g-2} L_d t^d + \frac{h q^g t^{2g-1}}{1 - qt} - \frac{h}{1 - t} \right). Proposition 3.1 (Functional Equation of the Zeta Function). Let X be a smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve of genus g over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q . Its local Zeta function satisfies the following symmetric functional equation: Z\left(X, \frac{1}{qt}\right) = q^{1-g} t^{2-2g} Z(X, t). Proof. We first establish a symmetry property for the sequence L_d . In the Picard group \operatorname{Pic}(X) , the map C \mapsto K - C (where K is the canonical divisor) provides a canonical bijection between \operatorname{Pic}^d(X) and \operatorname{Pic}^{2g-2-d}(X) . Using this bijection, we can rewrite the Riemann-Roch formula \ell(C) - \ell(K - C) = d + 1 - g as \ell(K - C) = \ell(C) - d - 1 + g . This allows us to directly relate L_{2g-2-d} to L_d : \begin{align*} L_{2g-2-d} &= \sum_{D \in \operatorname{Pic}^{2g-2-d}(X)} q^{\ell(D)} \\ &= \sum_{C \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X)} q^{\ell(K-C)} \\ &= \sum_{C \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X)} q^{\ell(C) - d - 1 + g} \\ &= q^{g-1-d} \sum_{C \in \operatorname{Pic}^d(X)} q^{\ell(C)} \\ &= q^{g-1-d} L_d \end{align*} Now, we substitute \frac{1}{qt} into the rearranged formula for Z(X, t) : Z\left(X, \frac{1}{qt}\right) = \frac{1}{q-1} \left( \sum_{d=0}^{2g-2} L_d (qt)^{-d} + \frac{h q^g (qt)^{1-2g}}{1 - q(qt)^{-1}} - \frac{h}{1 - (qt)^{-1}} \right). We will factor out q^{1-g}t^{2-2g} from each of the three terms inside the parenthesis to show they perfectly match the terms of the original Z(X, t) . First Term (The Finite Sum): We apply the substitution k = 2g - 2 - d . As d ranges from 0 to 2g-2 , k also ranges from 2g-2 down to 0 . Utilizing the symmetry L_{2g-2-k} = q^{g-1-k} L_k , we compute: \begin{align*} \sum_{d=0}^{2g-2} L_d (qt)^{-d} &= \sum_{k=0}^{2g-2} L_{2g-2-k} q^{-(2g-2-k)} t^{-(2g-2-k)} \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{2g-2} (q^{g-1-k} L_k) q^{-2g+2+k} t^{-2g+2+k} \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{2g-2} q^{1-g} L_k t^{2-2g+k} \\ &= q^{1-g} t^{2-2g} \sum_{k=0}^{2g-2} L_k t^k \end{align*} This exactly matches q^{1-g}t^{2-2g} times the first term of Z(X, t) . Second Term: We simplify the algebraic fraction: \begin{align*} \frac{h q^g (qt)^{1-2g}}{1 - q(qt)^{-1}} &= \frac{h q^g q^{1-2g} t^{1-2g}}{1 - t^{-1}} \\ &= \frac{h q^{1-g} t^{1-2g}}{(t - 1)/t} \\ &= \frac{h q^{1-g} t^{2-2g}}{t - 1} \\ &= -q^{1-g} t^{2-2g} \left( \frac{h}{1 - t} \right) \end{align*} This exactly matches q^{1-g}t^{2-2g} times the third term of Z(X, t) . Third Term: We simplify the final algebraic fraction: \begin{align*} - \frac{h}{1 - (qt)^{-1}} &= - \frac{h}{(qt - 1)/qt} \\ &= - \frac{h qt}{qt - 1} \\ &= \frac{h qt}{1 - qt} \\ &= q^{1-g} t^{2-2g} \left( \frac{h q^g t^{2g-1}}{1 - qt} \right) \end{align*} This exactly matches q^{1-g}t^{2-2g} times the second term of Z(X, t) . In conclusion, all three transformed terms precisely match the original terms of Z(X, t) multiplied by the scaling factor. We therefore obtain: Z\left(X, \frac{1}{qt}\right) = q^{1-g} t^{2-2g} Z(X, t). The functional equation is proved. ◻ The proof of the Second Part To estimate the lower bounds of sums of powers of complex numbers, which will be crucial for connecting the point counts to the roots of the Zeta function, we first require a foundational analytic lemma based on Dirichlet’s simultaneous approximation theorem. Lemma 3.1 (Integer Multiple Approximation of Phases). Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r be complex numbers with absolute value exactly equal to 1 . For any given real number \epsilon > 0 , there exist infinitely many positive integers m such that for all j = 1, \dots, r , we have: \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m) > 1 - \epsilon. Proof. We can write the complex numbers in polar form as \lambda_j = e^{2\pi i \theta_j} , where \theta_j \in \mathbb{R} . According to Dirichlet’s simultaneous approximation theorem, the sequence of fractional parts \left( \{m\theta_1\}, \dots, \{m\theta_r\} \right)_{m=1}^\infty must have an accumulation point in the r -dimensional torus (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^r . Because this is a translation on a compact group, the origin (0, \dots, 0) itself is an accumulation point. Therefore, for any arbitrarily small \delta > 0 , there exist infinitely many positive integers m such that for all j , the phase angle difference between \lambda_j^m and 1 on the unit circle is strictly less than 2\pi\delta . If we choose \delta to be sufficiently small such that \cos(2\pi\delta) > 1 - \epsilon , then by the geometry of the complex plane, we immediately obtain: \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m) = \cos(2\pi m \theta_j) > 1 - \epsilon. Since there are infinitely many such m for any \delta , the lemma is proved. ◻ Lemma 3.1 (Non-Degenerate Lower Bound for Power Sums). Let \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_t be a finite sequence of non-zero complex numbers. Then there exist infinitely many positive integers m such that: \left| \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m \right| \ge \max_{1 \le j \le t} |\alpha_j|^m. Proof. Without loss of generality, we may assume the complex numbers are sorted in descending order of their absolute values: |\alpha_1| = \dots = |\alpha_r| > |\alpha_{r+1}| \ge \dots \ge |\alpha_t|. Let this maximum absolute value be denoted by A = |\alpha_1| . We factor out the dominant magnitude A^m from the sum: \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m = A^m \left( \sum_{j=1}^r \left(\frac{\alpha_j}{A}\right)^m + \sum_{j=r+1}^t \left(\frac{\alpha_j}{A}\right)^m \right). Define normalized complex numbers \lambda_j = \alpha_j / A . By our ordering, for 1 \le j \le r , we have |\lambda_j| = 1 ; and for j > r , we have |\lambda_j| < 1 . Now, consider the real part of the normalized sum: \operatorname{Re}\left( \frac{1}{A^m} \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m \right) = \sum_{j=1}^r \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m) + \sum_{j=r+1}^t \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m). By Lemma , for any \epsilon > 0 (choose \epsilon < 1/r ), there exist infinitely many positive integers m such that the first sum strictly satisfies: \sum_{j=1}^r \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m) > r(1 - \epsilon). For the second term, because |\lambda_j| < 1 for all j > r , the geometric progression forces \sum_{j=r+1}^t \operatorname{Re}(\lambda_j^m) \to 0 as m \to \infty . Therefore, if we restrict our attention to the infinitely many chosen integers m , and take m sufficiently large, we must have: \operatorname{Re}\left( \frac{1}{A^m} \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m \right) \ge r(1 - \epsilon) - o(1) \ge 1. Because the real part of this complex number is greater than or equal to 1 , its absolute value must naturally be greater than or equal to 1 as well. This yields: \frac{1}{A^m} \left| \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m \right| \ge 1 \implies \left| \sum_{j=1}^t \alpha_j^m \right| \ge A^m = |\alpha_1|^m. This holds for infinitely many m , concluding the proof. ◻ Proposition 3.1 (Equivalence of the Riemann Hypothesis and Hasse-Weil Bound). Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over a finite field \mathbb{F}_q . We have shown its Zeta function takes the form: Z(X, t) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^{2g} (1 - \alpha_i t)}{(1 - t)(1 - qt)}. Let N_s denote the number of \mathbb{F}_{q^s} -rational points on X . Then the following two assertions are strictly equivalent: For all i = 1, \dots, 2g , the absolute value of the reciprocal roots satisfies |\alpha_i| = \sqrt{q} . There exists a constant c > 0 such that for all integers s \ge 1 , we have |N_s - q^s - 1| \le c \cdot q^{s/2} . Proof. We begin by explicitly extracting the point counts from the Zeta function. By definition, Z(X, t) = \exp\left( \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{N_s}{s} t^s \right) . Taking the formal logarithm of both sides and expanding the rational function representation: \begin{align*} \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{N_s}{s} t^s &= \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \log(1 - \alpha_i t) - \log(1 - t) - \log(1 - qt) \\ &= - \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{(\alpha_i t)^s}{s} + \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{t^s}{s} + \sum_{s=1}^\infty \frac{(qt)^s}{s} \end{align*} By equating the coefficients of t^s on both sides of the series, we instantly obtain the exact point-counting formula: N_s = q^s + 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i^s. Consequently, the deviation of the point count from the expected q^s + 1 is governed perfectly by the roots: |N_s - q^s - 1| = \left| \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i^s \right|. Proof of \Rightarrow : Assume holds, meaning |\alpha_i| = q^{1/2} for all i . Applying the standard triangle inequality to the deviation formula: |N_s - q^s - 1| = \left| \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i^s \right| \le \sum_{i=1}^{2g} |\alpha_i|^s = 2g \cdot q^{s/2}. Choosing the constant c = 2g immediately proves assertion . Proof of \Rightarrow : Conversely, assume holds. This means there exists some absolute constant c such that \left| \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i^s \right| \le c \cdot q^{s/2} for all s \ge 1 . We apply Lemma to the finite set of complex numbers \{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{2g}\} . Let \alpha_1 be a root with the maximal absolute value. By the lemma, there exist infinitely many integers s such that: |\alpha_1|^s \le \left| \sum_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i^s \right| \le c \cdot q^{s/2}. Taking the s -th root of both sides yields: |\alpha_1| \le c^{1/s} \cdot q^{1/2}. Because this inequality is satisfied for an infinite sequence of s tending to infinity, we can pass to the limit as s \to \infty . Since c^{1/s} \to 1 , we obtain: \max_i |\alpha_i| = |\alpha_1| \le \sqrt{q}. This proves that every root satisfies |\alpha_i| \le \sqrt{q} . On the other hand, in Theorem , we established that the polynomial P(t) = \prod_{i=1}^{2g} (1 - \alpha_i t) in the numerator has a leading coefficient of q^g . Expanding the product, the highest-order term is (-1)^{2g} \left( \prod_{i=1}^{2g} \alpha_i \right) t^{2g} . Therefore, the product of all reciprocal roots must exactly equal q^g : \prod_{i=1}^{2g} |\alpha_i| = q^g. If there were even a single root with |\alpha_i| < \sqrt{q} , then because absolutely no root can exceed \sqrt{q} (as proven above), the total product of their absolute values would be strictly less than (\sqrt{q})^{2g} = q^g . This directly contradicts the established leading coefficient. Therefore, the only mathematical possibility avoiding a contradiction is that for all i = 1, \dots, 2g , we have identically |\alpha_i| = \sqrt{q} . This completes the proof of equivalence. ◻ To apply the intersection theory of surfaces, we perform a base change to an algebraically closed field. Fix the finite field k = \mathbb{F}_q and choose its algebraic closure \bar{k} = \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q . Let X be a smooth projective irreducible curve over k . Let k = \mathbb{F}_q and \bar{k} = \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q be its algebraic closure. Let X be a separated scheme of finite type over k . Denote the base change by \bar{X} = X \times_k \bar{k} , and the product surface by S = \bar{X} \times_{\bar{k}} \bar{X} . Let F_X: X \to X be the absolute s -th Frobenius morphism, which is given on the structure sheaf by a \mapsto a^{q^s} . Its base change over \bar{k} is denoted by F^s = F_X \times_k \operatorname{id}_{\bar{k}}: \bar{X} \to \bar{X} . In S , the intersection of the diagonal scheme \Delta and the Frobenius graph scheme \Gamma_{F^s} is defined as the fiber product: Z = \Gamma_{F^s} \times_S \Delta Lemma 3.1 (Intersection Points Correspond to Rational Points). There exists a canonical one-to-one correspondence between the set X(k_s) = \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}k_s, X) and the set of \bar{k} -valued points of the intersection scheme Z , denoted by Z(\bar{k}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\bar{k}}(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, Z) . Proof. Given an intersection point z \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\bar{k}}(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, Z) . By the definition of the fiber product, giving z is uniquely equivalent to giving two morphisms u: \operatorname{Spec}\bar{k} \to \Gamma_{F^s} and v: \operatorname{Spec}\bar{k} \to \Delta such that their compositions in S are equal. From the constructions of \Gamma_{F^s} and \Delta in S , we have the following commutative diagram: The equality of the compositions of the morphisms u and v in S , namely \gamma \circ u = \delta \circ v , is equivalent to their equality under the two projections p_1, p_2 of S : \gamma \circ u = \delta \circ v \iff \begin{cases} p_1 \circ \gamma \circ u = p_1 \circ \delta \circ v \\ p_2 \circ \gamma \circ u = p_2 \circ \delta \circ v \end{cases} Since the closed immersions \gamma and \delta are defined by graph morphisms, the above equations simplify directly to: \iff \begin{cases} u = v \\ F^s \circ u = v \end{cases} \implies u = F^s \circ u Setting x = u = v , we obtain a morphism x \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\bar{k}}(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, \bar{X}) that satisfies: x = F^s \circ x \quad \text{--- (Eq. 1)} We note that x is a \bar{k} -morphism whose structure mapping is the identity map. The universal property of the fiber product induces the following canonical bijection: \operatorname{Hom}_{\bar{k}}(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, \bar{X}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, X) Geometrically, this means we have the following commutative diagram determined by the universal property: The mapping rule is x \mapsto x_X . According to the construction of the base change, the morphism can be decomposed as x = x_X \times_k \operatorname{id}_{\bar{k}} . Meanwhile, the geometric Frobenius F^s also takes the form F^s = F_X^s \times_k \operatorname{id}_{\bar{k}} . Substituting these two decompositions into (Eq. 1), on \bar{X} = X \times_k \bar{k} we have: x_X \times_k \operatorname{id}_{\bar{k}} = (F_X^s \circ x_X) \times_k \operatorname{id}_{\bar{k}} By the uniqueness of the adjoint bijection, this forces the following equality to hold in the set of k -morphisms of the original scheme X , \operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}\bar{k}, X) : x_X = F_X^s \circ x_X \quad \text{--- (Eq. 2)} We examine the affine open set U = \operatorname{Spec}A containing the morphism x_X .
